subtopic: IMPRISONMENT OP JACK REID FOR SEDITION.
speechtext:
1.	The prosecution of Reid was initiated and carried on by the local authorities. The information of this Government as to the words he pronounced is derived from the judge's charge, copy of which is hereto annexed.
2.	The Government has no information as to the words said to have been pronounced by Armand Lavergne, M.L.A., on the floor of the Quebec Legislative Assembly.

Rex vs. John Reid

Judge's Charge to the Jury
The Court: Gentlemen of the Jury, the defendant is charged with having used this language at three different meetings held in the province of Alberta, two held at Evarts and one at Rocky Mountain House, and he wishes to be tried by me alone, but I thought that this was eminently a case fitted for six jurymen, six citizens of this province to deliberate upon, because it is an offence of a somewhat peculiar nature. In regard to the majority of offences which are made indictable under our Criminal Code or under our law of Canada, there would be very little difference of opinion, I apprehend, and very few would express dissent to the fact that those things are made indictable offences, such as theft, arson and murder, but in regard to the offences charged it has some peculiar properties and is one where good common sense requires to be exercised in a remarkable degree, because there are certain principles which must be recognized and sometimes there may be an apparent conflict, of those principles; there may be a difficulty of adjustment so they may meet on a common ground; in other words, there may be some difficulty in a proper appreciation of just what a man may do and what he may not do when he is advocating political ideas or when he is discussing different forms of government-therefore, I thought that six men exercising the common sense which they have acquired through their knowledge of the world would be admirably fitted and even perhaps better fitted than I myself, to adjudicate upon so important a matter, so my duty will be to direct you on what I believe to be the law in relation to such offences and to call your attention to the evi'denoe adduced and the proper way to arrive at a correct conclusion. Then the matter will be one for you to determine as a question of fact.
When the authorities charge any person with an indictable offence under, our law, he is entitled to the presumption that he is innocent and the duty devolves upon the prosecution to

satisfy you beyond a reasonable doubt that the inferences you should draw, the only inference you can draw, is that he is guilty. If you are satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt then you are bound to bring in your verdict in accordance with that conclusion.
Now, there are some principles which must be recognized in adjusting yourselves to the proper viewpoint in connection with a charge of sedition. You have been told that the gist of the offence is speaking words of seditious intent and the Code has not described or attempted to define what seditious intent is, but the authorities are pretty well settled upon that and apparently it is to this effect, that any persons wishing to discuss public questions, questions affecting our Government institutions, affecting the authorities who administer those, they must do so within certain bounds. Counsel for the defence has quite properly called your attention to the well accepted principle applicable under British law and British institutions, and I may say particularly the British institutions, because it formed one of the central points of political discussion in England for a long time before the principle was eventually recognized and established, namely, that the subject of a Government had a proper right, the legal right to discuss and to criticise and even to condemn the Government if he thought the Government was dishonest or inefficient or the form of government was one which he believed was not the best one for his country; that principle is in force now and recognized by us that every subject has that right.
Some reference has been made to the religious opinons or the lack of religious beliefs of the defendant. That is also recognized in the British Dominion that a man has absolutely freedom of conscience as to the religious beliefs or lack of religious belief which he may adopt or profess and that is not to be charged against him.
Now, then, I think you may start with that as one of the accepted principles and one which must be kept in mind. There is another very important principle recognized and that is this that in order that any government may afford protection to life and property and even afford protection to that principle to which I have referred, namely:	(that
people shall have the right of freedom of speech and belief), there must be some authority to assert and protect that right therein ; that means there must be some administrative function, some form of government which will be able to so administer the law that we may have these privileges and that we may profess them without molestation assuming we are honestly professing them and adopting them for an honest purpose. Then you have those two principles and they may apparently meet and may apparently conflict when we come to discuss and decide just what is a seditious utterance or what are words which are capable of being charged as having a seditious intention, Every one must be presumed to intend the natural meaning and consequences and results of his words and his action, and I think that is peculiarly applicable to a man who assumes the responsibility of teaching or advocating or trying to enlighten others on political principles. I do not think he can complain if we assume he is a man who has undertaken to educate, to instill in others doctrines which he believes. Then he cannot be heard to complain if we say we will take him at his word,

and we will infer his intention in speaking these words from the natural meaning, the natural consequences of these words. Now I have already told you that in order that there may be an administrative function, some form of government which will be able to maintain law and order that involves that we shall not have in our community, in our country, riots, disturbances, tumults in places where people meet or assemble; and so then those who wish to express their opinions either by way of advocating any particular political opinion or by way of enlisting others must have that in view that they may be chargeable, if they speak words in times and places and of a nature that may have a tendency to incite people to opposition; to create in the people who hear them a spirit of hostility, to arouse feelings of animosity.^ I feel that as men of ordinary common sense it must be plain, it hardly needs to be argued, that words which will bring into contempt and scorn and ridicule those who are in high authority must be considered very very carefully by those who intend to utter them. I have already told you that people have the right to have that opinion even of those in high authority, even of members of the Government, even of the King, but the law requires a limit in this request that when they want to express these opinions to others they must have in view the fact that the law will not tolerate them expressing them under conditions which may create the feelings to which I have already referred, the feelings of animosity and hostility.
In regard to the words spoken at the three different meetings, the evidence is to the effect that they were spoken by the defendant in his capacity as an advocate of a party or an organization which I infer is of a political or semi-political nature. The defendant was holding meetings in the province of Alberta, in which he was discussing the principles which he believed should be applied and the form of government, or possibly the absence ' of form of government, although I have not heard any very clear expressions of the form of government. However generally we may say, that he claims to be the representative of the Socialist Organization of the province of Alberta, and he was advocating the principles of his organization, and I think it is only fair to say that he was doing that for the purpose of obtaining converts, of impressing people with his views and thereby turning people from their present opinions to his opinions, if they did not in the first instance agree with him.
Now the evidence is to the effect that in discussing these questions he dealt very pointedly with the present condition of things, with the state of war which now exists between our country and Austria and Germany, and he made certain statements at these different meetings which are pretty nearly the same. "Witnesses have sworn positively that he said he served in the Boer War and that he personally knew of British atrocities and the burning of Boer homesteads that were quite equal to any atrocities now charged against the Germans. Three witnesses have pledged their oath to that. They were unshaken in cross-examination and they say their minds were particularly impressed by that statement because they were apparently inclined to discredit it. They pledged their oath that their understanding of what was said was this, that the speaker, namely, the defendant, had served in the Boer war and knew these things by personal observation. The defendant

asks you to believe something different. He admits he was not on active service there, further than that he enlisted about the close of the war, and when he arrived with his company in South Africa the war was practically over. He says he didn't say these things at all, so either these people are mistaken or else he is not telling the truth. I think it is a fair observation to say that when a man at a public meeting who is advocating political principles makes a charge like that he should not make it in ambiguous language, he should not leave any doubt upon his audience as to whether he is speaking of personal knowledge or whether he is giving some other man's statement of it, because it is a pretty severe arraignment of Great Britain's methods if these things were true and these witnesses pledge their oath that they believed this defendant to be giving his own personal knowledge of these matters. He says he was not, that he was giving a statement of some one else. They pledge theif oath that he in discussing the present war charged the British soldiers with selling German fingers as souvenirs in Scotland and Paris, and that these were preserved in alcohol. He rebuts part of that statement and confines it, I believe, to an admission that he said such things were being done in Paris or somewhere in France. These people swear that he said, " We have nothing to be proud of that we have been born under the British flag, that we have no King or country. He served his country faithfully during the Boer war and then he travelled five thousand miles home to find he. didn't have a job, he didn't have a country, he didn't have a flag." His statement now here is that he didn't serve through the Boer war but reached there about the time the war was practically concluded. These witnesses swear positively that he made statements to the effect that this war was being carried on in the interests of the capitalists class who were really the inciting cause of the war. They also say he criticised the administration of the Patriotic Fund, saying that the proceeds would go the members of the . British Cabinet and the British Parliament. That these same were interested in an Armament Trust that had control of the armaments in both the Allies and Germany and Austria. He qualifies that now by saying that he was giving the opinion of another writer in that regard. They say further in their evidence that especially at the last meeting at which there were over a hundred present there was a very strong feeling, that the meeting was on the edge of a tumult. That to my mind is very important because that is one of the features which must be kept in mind very prominently in determining whether or not the defendant is guilty or not guilty of the charge. You are the absolute judges of the fact but I do not think it is an unfair comment for me to make when I say that might reasonably be expected, if at a time when our country is at war when great efforts are being made to enable the country to conduct this war to a successful conclusion, if some of the men holding public meetings, denounce those who are conducting the war, denounce their honesty and integrity and advocate that recruits should not join because those who are conducting the war have a vicious purpose in conducting it, then it seems to me those are things which might well agitate people and create a feeling of hostility and ill faith.
Now, gentlemen of the Jury, this is entirely a question of fact for you, having in mind the
directions which I have given you, and if in your opinion the purpose of these speeches or of any one of them, or any part of any one of them could fairly be considered to have in view the creation of a feeling of hostility for the purpose of bringing into contempt our administration, or any part of it or our army, or any part of it, or of those who are enlisting then it seems to me that the defendant has brought himself within the definition of the charge may be found guilty, if you come to that conclusion. The defendant seems to be a man who has travelled a good deal, you have heard him give his evidence. He seems to me a man who has made some study of the affairs of the world so he cannot have the benefit of this, that he was not able to appreciate and properly conclude what would be the reasonable effect of his words. He is apparently a somewhat clever young man, can speak quite fluently, can advocate his principles quite fluently and apparently is not lacking in intelligence at all and while granting him the right to hold political principles and to advocate them in a peaceful and proper way yet he must recognize the law as it exists. You, under your oath, must administer that law on the facts as you find them without fear or favour and as I have already observed I think it is a matter eminently fitting for six jurymen to adjudicate upon, not only for the purpose of the words spoken but the credibility of the defendant is in issue because in regard to some of the statements he has, as I have already observed, pledged his oath against the oath of the witnesses for the Crown. He is asking you te put a different construction on some of his statements from the construction which these men put upon them who heard them, and I have already told you that when people in public places for political or other purposes advocate things they are properly chargeable if people draw an inference which is a reasonable inference from the words spoken, and the words spoken have been so far as the evidence for the Crown is concerned, pretty well established. A good many of them have been admitted by the defendant. He has qualified them in a number of instances by saying these were not statements of his own knowledge but they were information from other sources. He has not given a very satisfactory explanation to my mind of the sources of the information in some of these regards. If he had them and is unable to have them now he is unfortunate but I am bound to make this observation that when a man in a public meeting attempts to instruct people or attemps to advocate political principles and make certain statements, I think he is under a duty to be able to give a reasonable substantiation of them when they purport to be statements acquired from some other source, especially when he makes wholesale charges which impute dishonest and improper motives to other citizens and when charged with making those statements he then says " well, I got them from some other source, from some newspapers or some journal ". I do not think we are asking too much of him if we expect him within reasonable bounds to produce the source of his information and if he does not make a reasonable explanation in that regard I think it is one of the items which may influence you properly in determining the credibility you will give to his statements in that regard.
Now, gentlemen of the jury, this is entirely and consider your verdict. It will be necessary for you to say under each count, there are

three counts charged and you can take them with you. It will be necessary for you to give a verdict on each of the three counts. In other words, give three verdicts, guilty or not guilty in each case.

May I be permitted to bring once again to the attention of the House the very important questiop of the rebuild,ing of our House of Commons? Immediately after the fire the Public Works Department undertook to make a general clean-up of the debris, which the House will understand was then so necessary for the purpose of recovering the bodies of the unfortunates who were lost as a result of the fire. This work has been done, and I regret to have to mention that which hon. members of the House know, that we have not, been able to discover the remains of our late fellow-member, Mr. Law.
I assumed the responsibility of selecting Mr. Pearson, of Toronto, and Mr. Marchand4 of Montreal, two very prominent architects, and asked them to come to Ottawa, first of all, to make a report on the condition of the walls as left standing after the fire, which report has already been submitted to the House. After they had completed that report I asked them to prepare preliminary plans along the lines which were thought most suitable for the rebuilding of the structure. The plans so prepared were inspected, I think, by most of the hon. members of this House yesterday afternoon, and, from what I have understood, they appear to meet with general acceptance.
We are now faced with the task of dividing the space in such manner as will be suitable to hon. members, as well as to the various officers connected with the work of the House, and now also comes immediately a further task for consideration, that of the form of contract und,er which the work of rebuilding is to be proceeded with. Altogether, many important points are involved which require prompt and careful consideration. In view of the fact that our House of Commons is a common ground for both parties at all times, I confess I hesitate, as Minister of Public Works, to assume the great task of undertaking to please everybody in connection with the

many points incident to the carrying out of the work, and I am, therefore, free to acknowledge that I feel the need of the friendly and sympathetic co-operation of both sides of the House. In the hope of being able to secure this, I am going to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister and the right hon. the leader of the Opposition to be good enough to name three members from each side of the House to act with me in thq making of all necessary arrangements for the immediate rebuilding of the House of Commons.

It is with
great pleasure that I say that, the work ' which has been done so far iby the Minister of Public Works has been quite satisfactory. We all acknowledge that in the manner in which he has provided for the temporary accommodation of members he has done his work as well as it could be done. With regard to the rebuilding of the Parliament Buildings, so far I am happy to say that I can also express my approval. The selection by the Minister of Public Works of the two architects, Mr. Pearson and Mr. Mar-chand, was eminently judicious, as both of those gentlemen stand very high in their profession. Yesterday I, with many other hon. members, inspected the plans which have been prepared by these two architects, and I at once expressed to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works my satisfaction that therp is to be no change in the outside appearance of those buildings. A fact which I think every one will agree is most desirable. We all have a kindly regard for those buildings; they were of great beauty, and their beauty will not be marred by the plans of the architects.
As to the interior of the buildings, I would not speak with so< much confidence, but for my part I have no criticism to offer. So far as I could judge-I acknowledge my incompetence-the improvements suggested will certainly add to the beauty of the interior of the buildings and to the comfort of the members generally. I have only to add that I shall be glad to confer with my right hon. friend the Prime Minister as to the committee.

It is, of course, very difficult for one who is not an expert to understand from a mere inspection of the plans what a building will be when completed. So far as one is capable of judging, it seems to me that the plan proposed is the best possible that could be devised, unless indeed we should alter the external
appearance of the building, which I entirely agree with my right hon. friend should be avoided, if possible. The gentlemen who have very seriously devoted themselves to the work of preparing the plan are both very eminent in their profession. The plan which they have eventually adopted is not the one which they first suggested, but it is the result of much study and consideration with a view to preserving the former appearance of the building and at the same time of securing more adequate accommodation for the Senate 'and for the Conimons. A great many things will have to be taken into consideration in connection with the present plan, as to the location of the numerous offices which are necessary for carrying on the business of the House in a convenient way; but I understand from the architects, with whom I have spoken on the subject, that there will be more accommodation of that kind available under the proposed plan than there was in the building as it was before the fire. Therefore I think that we may congratulate ourselves, not only upon the selection of the two architects who have undertaken the work, but also upon the success which seems to have crowned their endeavours, and which I hope will be fully realized when the building is once more ready for occupation by the two Houses of Parliament. I shall, of course, be very glad to name three of my colleagues to co-operate with and assist the Minister of Public Works in conjunction with the gentlemen who shall be selected from the other side of the House.

Is it intended that this committee shall have any duties beyond giving theiT opinion as to the best mode of laying out the new buildings and as to the accommodation to be afforded? >Is it in- [DOT] tended that the committee shall have to do with the letting of the contract; and, generally, the work of reconstruction? It is important to have it understood, whether the Minister of Public Works would desire to vest in the committee some form of control and responsibility as to how the work is to be done, whether by tender or by day's work, or whether their duties shall be limited to designing the proper lay-out of the building.

If the hon. gentleman will read my statement as reported in Hansard,
I think he will find that I covered that point.

I desire to say a word on behalf of the private members of this

House, because in my capacity as one of the Whips, I have had many complaints as to the inadequacy of the accommodation given to private members. In many cases, eight, nine, and even ten members are crowded into one room. In my opinion, there is no reason why the private members of this House, who are supposed to be representative men in their several constituencies, should be compelled to occupy quarters here which they would not occupy at home. Whatever provision is made for the Ministers of the Crown and the officials, I hope the committee will see to it that if each member of the House is not given a separate room, at least the number of members occupying a room shall be reduced to a minimum. We must not forget that in the near future the House of Commons will have ten per cent more members than it now has. I think that members are entitled to more spacious quarters than they have had, even if it should cost half a million dollars more to provide proper accommodation in the new building, which will be designed to last for all time. I believe that the people would desire that their representatives should be reasonably accommodated.

According to the report
of the architects, there will be at least thirty-eight per cent more space in the new building than in the old. That being the case, I am sure that provision of an adequate character will be made for the requirements of the members of the House. That, I am sure, will be the first duty of the committee.

speechtext:
I really am
afraid it will be impossible to so re-arrange the new building that every member will have a room to himself. While it is desirable to give to the members all accommodation possible, we older members of Parliament know that formerly no rooms were provided for private members of the House. During the first five years I was in Parliament, I think that not more than ten per cent of the members had any accommodation in the way of a room. The older members were given the few rooms that were available at that time. About ten years ago, we began for the first time to make an endeavour to give private members some accommodation outside the Commons Chamber. I agree, of course, that we should endeavour to make the accommodation as extensive and as comfortable as possible.

On the motion of Sir Robert Borden for
Committee of Supply:

Before you leave
the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the Government some statements that I have seen in the press. In the Montreal Gazette of yesterday it was stated that the Minister of Militia and Defence, who is now in, England, was going to reorganize the Canadian forces in England, and, I think, at the front as well. I see in to-day's Citizen a statement of a similar character, as follows:
One correspondent with unaffected simplicity asked the general if he meant soon to lead the Canadians into Berlin.
"Well," said Sir Sam, "if Douglas Haig goes I am going with him."
The general-
That is, the Minister of Militia and Defence.
-had an interview to-day with Lord Kitchener at the War Office, and will hold a conference of the Canadian brigadiers at his hotel tomorrow morning, when the whole question of a reorganization of the forces will be discussed.
The word "forces" is used; that would mean the forces in England and at the front as well. The forces in England and at the front are under the direction of the military authorities, and if they need reorganization, that would presuppose that there is now disorganization, which would be a very serious matter indeed. I think that question as to whether these statements are correct is worthy of serious consideration by the House and by the Government. If the Minister of Militia and Defence had to go to the old country for that purpose, there would be a state of chaos over there; but I hope it is not that bad. A short time ago I saw in the Toronto Telegram an intimation to the effect that while the Minister of Militia and Defence was in the United States some of the military authorities there consulted him with regard to military matters in that country, and that he put things right in a few moments. Of course, that is a matter of pride to every Canadian. But the question is:	Can the country at the present time
afford the absence of the Minister of Militia and Defence, who is so well qualified to organize even the military forces of the United States? A short time ago, after an order had been received from Great Britain for the sending of 20,000 troops to the old country, it was stated by the Militia Department, I think, that a good deal of disorganization had been discovered in Canada. Some of the older regiments that had been drilling for quite a considerable time were not up to strength and were not ready to leave for Great Britain on short notice. In consequence, some of the regiments that were in a 'higher state of efficiency, although they had been in training for a shorter time, had to be taken. That would show that there was some lack of organization here. It is strange, therefore, that the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) should be able to organize our forces in Great Britain, and to give useful information to the military authorities in the United States, but could not keep up the organization here. Of course, these are only newspaper reports, but they are contained in newspapers supporting the Government, and they may disturb the public mind.
In the Montreal Gazette of yesterday I see a further reference to the visit of the Minister of Militia to the Old Country. I understand that this country is paying to the Canadian Associated Press some $15,000 a year for news from Great Britain. That is quite a sum of money, and if it is spent in proportion to the length of the telegrams that come to Canada and not in proportion to the quality of the news they contain, some discrimination should be exercised. This telegram, a column long, in the Montreal Gazette, treats of what I consider trivial matters. One paragraph says:
The Canadian Minister drove Ho the library in a limousine occupying a seat beside the mayor, who wore his full regalia of office. After inspection of the guard of honor, Sir Sam Hughes reviewed a parade of school cadets numbering several hundred. At the request of the distinguished visitor, a half holiday was granted to the pupils of the public schools.
While that may be of interest to some people, it is not a matter of general importance to the country, and if we havb to pay for it and other news of the same kind, there will be trouble. I do not think the people of Canada will care to contribute to the cost of cabling that class of news. I bring this matter to the attention of whatever minister can control it. There is considerable advertising of the Minister of Militia going on. I noticed this paragraph in

the Citizen, copied from the Montreal News:
How Canada was almost deprived forever of the services of her Minister of Militia and the world of its greatest character actor, was told by Mr. Cyril Maude when seen last night.
The important matter to which I direct attention is that there has apparently been such disorganization in the Canadian forces that it was necessary for the Minister of Militia and Defence to go to the Old Country to bring about a reorganization. That is a most important and serious matter, if the statement is correct.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. E. KEMP (Acting Minister of Militia):
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has referred to certain honours that have been conferred upon the Minister of Militia and Defence, both in the United States and in Great Britain, to which, I suppose, he does hot take any objection. The freedom of the city of Falmouth was conferred upon the minister, according to a newspaper report, which I presume is correct. The hon. gentleman would not take any objection to that?
No, I am only taking objection if we have to pay for the cabling of all this news.

I have no information as to who paid for the conveyance in which the minister rode. I presume the hon. gentleman was not in the House when the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition asked a question in regard to the duties of the Minister of Militia in England, and was answered by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government. I do not think I could say any more on that subject than was said by the Prime Minister.

Post Office Department-Outside Service, salaries and allowances, $7,943,152.25.

Mr. Chairman, I am really sorry that the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) is not here this afternoon, and I would gladly have postponed the consideration of the Estimates of the Post Office Department were it not that I believe it would be inconvenient and not in the public interest, because if I did so we would probably not have enough business to place before the House to-day. The committee

will allow me, before taking up this item, to make a statement as to the expenditure of the department within the last few years. I shall do so because dt seems to me that the committee is entitled to an explanation of certain items of the expenditure as to which criticism has been directed. I may say that a great deal -of the criticism which has been levelled at the department is due to incorrect information, and I am convinced that I will be able to show that a large proportion of the increase of expenditure is not due to any mal-administratdon of the affairs of the department, but is due in some cases to uncontrollable circumstances, and in others to increase cost of the service which were voted by this House, and concurred in by both sides. I shall also endeavour to show that I have done the best I could, and that the department is doing the b?st it can, to curtail expenditure. Hon. gentlemen opposite will, I think, acknowledge that my colleagues and I are alive to the very grave circumstances which at present exist, and that we are convinced that, if ever strict economy was necessary, it is necessary to-day. It is a well known fact that the expenditure of the Post Office Department has always increased from year to year. There has not been a year since Confederation in which there has not been a large increase in the expenditure of the Post Office Department over the preceding year, for the reason that the country is growing and that, with the growth of the country, it has been necessary to give to the people a more perfect and more extended postal service. If we look at the figures given in the Post Office Report, we will see, for instance, that in 1897 the expenditure of the Post Office Department was $3,789,478; whilst in 1912 it was $9,172,035, being an increase during those years of $5,382,557. Nobody, I believe, will say that that increase was not justified. But let me draw the attention of the committee to the fact that during all those years no reform which involved an increased expenditure was -introduced. Reforms were introduced in the service, I am free to admit, but in comparison with what had been done during the previous four or five years in the department, there were none of those changes or alterations in the service which would bring about any great increase in the expenditure of the department. There has been an increase, and a considerable increase in the expenditure of the department within the last four years, but I think I

can account for almost every cent of that increased expenditure.
Let me take, for instance, rural mail delivery, which has been mentioned in this House several times. This service was inaugurated, I freely admit, by my hon. friend the member for Bouville (Mr. Lemieux), and he is entitled to due credit for it, and when it proved beneficial and advantageous to the country, it was our bounden duty to follow out the lines which were laid down by my predecessor, in order to carry the system to the perfect state in which it is to-day. The United States inaugurated a rural mail service in 1897, with 82 routes; to-day there are 44,373 rural mail routes in the United States, which cost the enormous sum of $49,625,000. Last summer I visited the United States to inquire into their system; I made a trip to some of the states for that purpose, and I am proud to say that I found that our service is in every respect superior to the system in the United States, and that it costs much less. In the United States every patron purchases his own box; therefore there is a diversity of boxes. Not only that, but he is permitted to place the box on any part of his farm, so that every time the mail carrier goes round, he has to get out of his vehicle to collect the postal matter in the box and when delivering letters to the boxes he has to do the same thing. Our boxes are so made that the carrier is not obliged to leave his vehicle. Another thing I found in the United States was that the man in a great many cases carried the mail either on the seat alongside of him or in the bottom of his vehicle, whereas in Canada the mail carrier is provided with a bag, and when he comes to the gate, without getting out of the vehicle, and therefore without danger of losing any mail matter, he simply takes it out of, the box and places it in the bag. Our boxes instead of being as they are in the United States furnished by each patron,
v4 p.m. according to the make which he thinks the best, are furnished by the Government at almost cost price.
It is an open box?

It closes, but it does
not lock. We have come to the conclusion, and the experts in the service have come to the conclusion, that it would delay the mails greatly if the man were obliged at every collection to unlock and relock the box.
We have in Canada at the present time,
3,337 rural mail routes, divided by provinces as follows:	Prince Edward Island,
168; Nova Scotia, 127; New Brunswick, 219; Quebec, 633; Ontario, 1,904; Manitoba, 86; Saskatchewan, 56; Alberta, 82; and British Columbia, 62; making the total 3,337. The number of rural mail routes established in each province during the last fiscal year, from 1st April, 1914, to 31st March, 1915, , was as follows: Prince Edward Island, 23; Nova Scotia, 27; New Brunswick, 47; Quebec, 233; Ontario, 292; Manitoba, 30; Saskatchewan, 11; Alberta, 21; British Columbia, 11; making a total of 695. From 1st April, 1915, to the end of February, 1916, the number of rural routes established was 425, divided as follows:	Prince Edward
Island, 11; Nova Scotia, 26; New Brunswick, 15; Quebec, 207; Ontario, 99; Manitoba, 16; Saskatchewan, 18; Alberta, 23; and British Columbia, 10.
The total increased cost to the department by the establishment of the rural routes within the past three years is $855,000, so that one of the items in the increased expenditure of the Post Office Department is accounted for by the establishment of rural mail routes which I think the committee will agree are for the general advantage of our people.

What is the average increased cost as between the rural mail service in any one section, and the former mail service in the same district? The figures which the minister has given do not convey very much information to the committee.

I will try to give all
the information required as I go along. I cannot give my hon. friend the information he asks for just at this moment, but $855,000 was the increase in the cost in the three years over the old system.

What is the increase
for the whole period?

That is the increase
for the whole period. .

What was it last
year?

I will give the hon.
member that information later'.

Can the minister give us some idea as to the system or grounds upon which those rural mail routes are established? According to the figures which he read, giving the number in the different provinces, Prince Edward Island, with a



small population, has pretty nearly as many routes as the province of Nova Scotia.

The routes are established by the officer in charge. When a demand is made for a rural mail service the officer visits the district and if 50 per cent of the inhabitants along the route ask for the establishment of a rural mail, it is given to them. Why there are almost as many in the province of Prince Edward Island as there are in Nova Scotia, I cannot say, except that in the province of Prince Edward Island more routes may have been asked for than in the province of Nova Scotia.

What is the principle
upon which the post offices are closed?

When a rural mail
route is established in a locality my hon. friend will understand that the patrons of that route have no more use, or very little use, for'the post office.
The post office in New Richmond West has been there for sixty years.

That may he. I am having that matter looked into, and if there is any good reason why an exception to the rule should be made in this ease the post office will not he closed. I would, point out that the people interested in this particular post office now get their mail delivered right at their doors.
There is a Model school right along the post office, and the children used to take the letters home with them.

That is a sentimental reason, to a great extent. As I pointed out, the people whose children used to go to the Model school and take their letters home from the post office can now get their letters right at their doors. The great question to consider is the general interest of the community. If it is to the advantage of the community that the post office should be kept open, why, then, it should be kept open. We are looking into this particular case, and if there is any substantial reason why that post office should not be closed it will not be closed-
An additional reason why it should not be closed is that under the old system the incoming and outgoing mail was handled on the same day. Under the new system there is a d,elay of twenty-four hours.

The people should have weighed all these considerations before they asked for a change. Nobody forced them to accept rural mail delivery. Of course, there are always some people who will be dissatisfied, but it is the general advantage of the community that must govern. In addition to the sum of $855,000 which I mentioned a little while ago, there is the sum of $305,000 for boxes purchased during those three years.
The patrons pay for the boxes.

But the expenditure
has to be met. These boxes cost us $305,000.

For the whole
period?
Yes. If you add these two sums together you have a total' of $1,160,000, which was expended on the extension of the rural mail service throughout Canada.
The department gets the money back for those boxes.

In the first place, we
have to buy the boxes. Then we sell them to the public practically at cost price. The price to the public just covers the cost of the box, and the cost of putting the boxes up, plus carrying charges.

The minister has given the cost of the boxes for a period of three years. If we had the figures for each year, we should then be able to study the comparative revenue and expenditure of the department. I think those figures might ,be useful to us.

I will bring those
figures down.
And the amount the department has received from the sale of these boxes.

I will bring that down too. Hon. gentlemen will, I hope, bear with me if I cannot give them all the details to-day. The department which I administer is a very large one, employing in the city of Ottawa alone 800 employees.
There are 19,000 postmasters and 23,000 employees. The department extends from one end of the Dominion to the other. I must admit that there are a great many details I have not mastered yet, but I am perfectly willing, and indeed it is my duty,

to give to the House all the iiaormation it asks for. But hon. gentlemen must be a little patient with me if I cannot give this information off-hand. In view of the absence of my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) my intention was not to finally dispose of this discussion to-day; so I shall have another opportunity to bring down the information that has been asked for.
Another advantage of our system over that of the United States'is that all contracts for the carrying of mail are let by public tender. The statement has been made in the House that under the regiqie of my immediate predecessor this system of letting contracts by public tender had been cast to the winds; but, I can find no warrant for such a statement. When I took charge of the department I found that the system of public tender had always been followed; and ever since I have been in office the rule has been followed of letting mail contracts by public tender.

Let me give an instance of how it was done in Carleton, in the county of Bonaventure. The man who had carried the mails there for years put in a tender a few days before his contract lapsed. Another man put in a tender at a higher figure, and this latter man was told that if he would reduce his price to the other man's figure he would get the contract. He did so and got the contract.

If the minister will look at the files of his own department he will find that a return was laid on the table of the House in the first year after the Conservatives came to office, showing that over 500 mail contracts were cancelled during that first year. The return shows that a great many of the contracts which had not expired when this Government took office were cancelled when they came in, and new contracts given to their friends. There was an example in my own county, which has perhaps the largest mail contract in Nova Scotia. The contract was let in the first place by public tender, and the service was quite satisfactory. When this Government came in, the contract was cancelled, and turned over by them to one of their friends. The minister will find that on record in his own department.

I will look it up. I can tell my hon. friend that the rule of the department is that no contract of that kind is to be given out without public tender. The great fault found with us is that the prices are too low, and we are
127}	.
receiving complaints, not only from this side of the House, but from hon. members on the other side, that the amounts paid to the mail carriers are not sufficient. That is the general complaint throughout the country, and I have scores upon scores of letters in my office giving 'various reasons as to why the rate should be increased. The matter was discussed last year when the Estimates of the Post Office Department were before the House. One reason that is being continually given for an increase in the wages of the mail carriers is that the inauguration of the parcel post system has entailed more work upon them. The statement which has been made that the system of public tender for mail contracts has been cast to the winds, is not borne out by the facts.

What is the good of having a system of public tender if you do not award contracts to the lowest tenderer? The system of tendering is one thing, but the matter of abiding by the result of the tenders is another, and there are hundreds and thousands of cases-
Steady.
-in Canada which hon. gentlemen on this side of the House could present, showing that contracts were not awarded to the lowest tenderer.
Name them.
We have given 500 such cases
Just one.
No.
With all deference to my hon. friend from Halifax, I think his statement is exaggerated. The rule is that none of those contracts shall be given out without public tenders being called for.

Is it not a fact that, after tenders have been received, an opportunity is given to the man who has the patronage in the county to inform a higher tenderer that, if he will reduce his tender so as to make it equal to the lowest tender, he will get the contract? I know of a number of such instances in my county. That is not fair.	*

I do not agree with my hon. frienc( that that is not fair, because no one could complain that the public interest suffers if the lowest tender is $500 and an opportunity is given to some one

else to tender below that. My hon. friend says that is not fair. Well, I do not think so.
I did not say '"below," I said "the same figure."
Then my hon. friend is wrong, because X know that in certain cases the contract has been 'let at a lower .figure.
Sometimes a dollar less.

If a tender has been sent in for $500, and information is received that the work can be done for $480, surely no one can complain that the public interest suffers, if, instead of the contract being given to some one at $500, it is given to some one else at $480.
Political patronage is served.

If the Postmaster General will permit me, I think I can show him where the public interest does suffer. It has become generally known in certain districts of the province of Nova Scotia that it is practically useless for Liberals to tender for mail contracts, because the moment tenders are in and it is found that a Liberal is the lowest tenderer, the man having the patronage of the county corresponds with the Post Office Department recommending the name of a Conservative wiho will do the work for a few dollars less, or for the same figure, and he gets the contract. Therefore, I say that the public interest has suffered inasmuch as public confidence is lessened in the system of tender and contract as carried out by the Post Office Department.
I do not think that the public interest has suffered; I think the Liberal party has suffered.

The public interest has suffered inasmuch as you have ceased to get the competition of those who otherwise would put in tenders, because one portion [DOT]of the community refuses to put in tenders knowing that they will not receive a contract. Therefore in certain sections there is practically no competition with regard to the letting of contracts for the mail service.
Let me cite a case in my constituency. The mail service between Grandique Ferry, West Arichat, and Arichat had been performed for twenty years by a man named Parker for, I think, $480 a year. He died and his widow carried on the service for
[Mr. Casgrain.l
about a year and then tenders' were called for. Six tenders were received, the lowest being in the neighbourhood of $600. Five of the tenders were Conservatives; the lowest tenderer was a Liberal. The contract was not awarded. It was claimed by the department that the tenders were too high. I endeavoured to point out to the officials of the department that the work could not be carried on as cheaply as twenty years ago. The service called for the carriage of the mail twice a day between those post offices, and the lowest tenderer was then Risked to put in a tender for performing a trip a day only. He put in a tender for $345. A contract was then executed between him and the Post Office Department and he is carrying the mail now one trip each day for $345 a year. When the steamboat is not Tunning, it is necessary to have a trip made in the morning, and the department has engaged another man to make that trip, so that there are now two contractors instead of one. The department objected to giving the contract to this man Murray for $550 or $600 because they thought his tender was too high. They are, however, paying him $345 a year for making one trip a day, and they are paying another man for performing the morning trip whenever it is necessary. It is surely not in the public interest that the contract should be divided up in that way. I ven-. ture to say that the cost of carrying the mail between these offices under the present system will amount to very much more than the original lowest tender.
I would ask my hon. friend to draw my attention to that matter, and I will look into it.
You will be doing nothing else for the next year if you look up such matters.
Is the minister going to pronounce judgment in regard to the matter?
I am not going to pronounce judgment before I know the facts. I have heard only one side of the case; I shall have to hear the other side before I pronounce judgment.

I understood the minister to say a few minutes, ago that, if the public interest did not suffer, he felt quite justified in disregarding the system of tender and contract, that is, the question of who was the lowest tenderer or not, so long as some one got the contract at the lowest tender price.

That was not my argument. I said that no one could complain that the public interest suffered because one man did not get a contract at $500, if some one else got it at $480. I am not going to pronounce upon any abstruse question of policy in regard to the Post Office Department; I have enough to do to look into the concrete cases. I will examine into the case which my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has brought to the attention of the House, and, after looking into it, I shall be able to say whether or not I approve what was done in the circumstances.
What will be done if the minister does not approve?
On further consideration, I will see what I shall do.
There are two men doing one man's work now.

I do not know about that. There have been statements made by hon. members opposite in connection with the Post Office Department which, with all due deference to my hon. friends, are, to say the least, exaggerated. I do not say that the statement made by my hon. friend from Richmond is exaggerated, but I think I should be given an opportunity of looking into the matter before pronouncing judgment upon it.
Will the hon. gentleman say that if he finds a mistake has been made he will correct it?

I will not say anything before having the facts before me. I am not going to give judgment on a state of facts of which I know nothing; and, as 1 say, I have enough to do with the concrete cases that come before me for decision, without attempting to deal with the abstract cases put before me by hon. gentlemen opposite.

I would submit to the hon. gentleman a concrete case, that of Napoleon LeBlane, at Carleton, Que., a man who gave faithful service, and who was recommended by the whole municipality. He was thrown aside and replaced! by another who did the work for some months and then threw up the job, with the result that the department had no carrier at all. LeBlane wras asked to take it again, which, after persuasion, he did. But soon after he was again thrown out and tne contract was given to a new man,
who does not do the work, but has it done by a young boy.
Mr. CASGRAIN-:- Is it badly done?

I do not know what the department says about that, but the people there say that this is not by any means the way to encourage faithful service. I would like to know what the department says about that case. In that connection I would ask if there is a Tule of the department that contracts below a certain minimum may be given without tender.

These changes were made by Parliament in adopting certain statutes in 1912, 1913, and 1914. In 1912, by statute 2, George V, Chapter 14, salaries were considerably increased. For instance, the fourth class, with salaries of from $400 to $700 was abolished, and a minimum of $500 and a maximum of $900 were established. A senior class, with a minimum of $1,000 and a maximum of $1,500 was replaced by a first class with a minimum of $1,400 and a maximum of $1,800. Under the old Act the statutory increases were of $50 per annum, whilst by the new Act the increases in salaries up to $800 were fixed at $100 per annum. In 1913, an Act was passed under which all letter carriers, messengers and porters in city post offices were divided into five gradings. This Act raised the minimum from $1.75 a day to $2 a day, and gave the employees an increase of 25 cents a day each year, instead of every two years, until a maximum of $3 a day was reached. The maximum was attained in five years, instead of ten years as under the old Act. The' same Act gave an increase of $100 a year to all railway mail clerks who had been fifteen years or longer in the service. When Sir William Mulock became head of the Post Office Department, like the present minister, he had his difficulties; and he grappled with them in a masterly way. cerned; the period during which her population rapidly increased, and the great West largely developed- At the end of that period Canada, as a commercial country, as a hive of industry, and as a rapidly developing agricultural country, was no longer on the back street among the nations of the world, but on the front street. During those fifteen years, with all the progress and development that was taking place, the increase in the number of post office employees was 1,385. On October 1, 1911, the number of employees was 2,208. On February 1, 1916, there were 3,640 employees in the Post Office Department. I think that substantiates the indirect criticism of the Postmaster General that his predecessor had loaded this department beyond all reason.

The increase in the number of employees during the fifteen years previous to 1911 was 217; the increase during the last four years was 113, a little over half as many. I need not say anything as to that western city which during the fifteen years previous to 1911, went ahead by leaps and bounds, and is doing so now, I presume. It has had a marvellous growth and extension; but although those figures are much nearer what they ought to be than the figures in some of the other cities that I have mentioned, still I think reasonable men will agree with me that there has been no greater ratio of increase in Winnipeg during the last four years than there was during the

previous fifteen years when Winnipeg grew to be the Winnipeg that it is to-day.

By what process of argument? The hon. gentleman, of course, will see that an increase of twenty-five per cent in a city of 50,000 people would call for a smaller increase of post office employees than would an increase of twenty-five per cent in a city of 100,000 people. The hon. gentleman's argument has no force for the additional reason that eastern cities, such as Montreal, Toronto, Quebec, and others, have grown within the last five or six years equally with the western cities, or, in some cases, even more.
I fear I do not catch the hon. gentleman's argument.

The hon. gentleman says that in so many years 150 men were added, but in the last five or ten years two hundred and fifty men were added. That may be perfectly right as a statement of fact, but the conclusion which the hon. gentleman draws from it does not necessarily follow. The growth during the last four years would be much greater in numbers than during the ten years before, though the percentage might be the same. For instance, the number of people added to the population of Toronto from 1890 to 1900 would :be, possibly, 60,000, which would require an increase, let us say, of 100 in the number of post office employees. But if the city increased in similar ratio in the next ten years, the increase possibly would be 150,000 and the additional number of post office employees would need to be in proportion. Does not the hon. gentleman see that?

I hear the hon. gentleman's statement, but I am not impressed with it. His argument does not need any reply from me, for the reason that the Postmaster General has already replied by saying that the number of employees was too great and that he had reduced the number.	*
I did not say it was too great.

But he did say that he had reduced the number? If he has not made any reduction, then I will have to take back all the compliments I offered
him.

The circumstances under which we are now operating are absolutely different from those when Mr. Pelletier

was head of the department. I am not going to say that he employed too many men. I say that the circumstances under which we are now living make necessary the strictest economy, and so, if I have reduced the number of employees even at the expense of the employees, they will have to make the sacrifice.

The hon. gentleman is generous to his predecessor, and I admire him for it, but the fact Temains that he has taken pains, in, the statement he has made to the House, to divide it into two parts, one covering the period when his predecessor was in office, and the other under his own administration. This is a thing unprecedented in governments, for the Government is responsible no matter how ministers may change; it is not customary to divide the actions of Government as between a minister and his successor. I appreciate my hon. friend's gentility and his tenderness to his predecessor. I am only showing that he has grounds for his action, and he cannot get away from that very well. In St. John post office, the total number of employees on the 1st of February last was 95, as compared with 72 in October, 1911, and 56 in July, 1896; an increase in fifteen years of 16 employees, and in the last four years of 23. In Halifax post office there were 93 employees on the 1st February last, as against 71 in October, 1911, and 47 in, July, 1916; an increase in fifteen years of 24 and an increase within the last four years of 22.

I notice that the hon. gentleman is making a comparison of fifteen years with the last four years. Has he the figures to enable him to make a comparison of the last four years and the four years immediately preceding?
I have not those figures, but I think if I had them I should not be alarmed by the reading of them.

Has the hon. gentleman the figures to show the relative growth of population and of post office employees? That would enable us to judge whether there had been more than a normal increase. For instance, Saskatoon, fifteen years ago, probably required only one person in the post office, even if theTe was a post office at all. I know that there were only about three houses when I was first there.

I have not gone into
that. But I may say that the complaint ia that din many of these cities the population has not increased so rapidly within the last few years as in some years previously. But perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie) had better not make selections, as he might be unhappy in some of them.

But would it not be
fair?
' Mr. GRAHAM: It might be, but I have not the figures before me. I want to emphasise what the Postmaster General made clear to my mind this afternoon, that, while, previous to 1914, there evidently has been an overmanning of the department, he, since 1914, bad been doing his best to bring the expenditure down, and that in doing so he had reduced the number of employees.
During the war period.

The beginning of the wai period synchronized with the change of ministers. But the hon. gentleman went further, and stated very strongly that not only had he reduced the number of employees, but he proposed to reduce them stall further; that he intended to make appointments only when absolutely necessary; and that where there was not work for the present employees he would gradually dispense with the services of some of them. He told us, inferehtially, that he would have dispensed with the services of some but for the fact that it would not have been humane to deprive them of their employment abruptly. In that, I have a good deal of sympathy with him. If I may understand anything from his remarks, my understanding is that the department was overmanned, that he had been reducing the staff gradually, and proposed to get it to a business basis. In that I think he is to be commended. The figures I have given, compiled from his own .answers to questions, I think, speak for themselves, and are a proof of his wisdom in carrying out the policy he has announced.
