speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Graham) has referred to the post office at St. John, showing that there has been an increase of .something over twenty in the number of employees since 1911. The postmaster at St. John, Mr. Sears,, has been postmaster since 1908 or 1909, and, so far as I know, he has been a good postmaster and has given veTy good satisfaction to the public. I think the correspondence will , show

that any increase in the number of employees in St. John post office has been made on the direct representation of the postmaster who has pointed out from time to time what clerks wiere necessary in order to properly do the work of the post office there. The clerks are appointed on the recommendation of the postmaster, after investigation by the officials of the department. Speaking from what I know-and I would know if the reverse were the base -*since 1911 the Post Office Department has never been urged to appoint post office clerks for party reasons or for party purposes. Such appointments have been made at the instance of the postmaster who decided what clerks were needed to handle properly the postal business of the city of St. John.
Since 1911 there has been a considerable increase in the population of the city of St. John, although that, perhaps, would not account for the total increase. At the St. John office mails are received and despatched to other points throughout New Brunswick and the Maritime Provinces; the increase in the work in that connection has necessitated the employment of a number of additional clerks. Further, until a few years ago, the Atlantic mails during the winter months went through the city of Halifax. Most of these mails now go through the port of St. John, and that necessitates the appointment of more clerks than were previously required. The increase has been made for public reasons, and not at all for party purposes. From what I can learn, I do not think that there are too many officials in the post office at St. John properly to do the work required of them. They are hard working men, and their hours are long. The number that my hon friend has mentioned includes the members of the letter carrier staff; in order to discharge properly the work of distributing letters throughout the city, it has been found necessary by the postmaster on several occasions to urge in the strongest possible way that an increase be made in his staff. The increases have always been made upon his instance, and not for party purposes.

I should like to ask the hon. member for South Renfrew whethei it is not possible to inject into this discussion some reference to the expansion oi trade. Surely the matter of population and the record of the number of persons previously employed are not the only elements in the question. We have had a tremend-

ous expansion of facilities for the public, such as parcel post and rural mail delivery. Since 1911 the trade of the country has increased, I think, more than 25 per cent; therefore the natural inference would be that the number of employees required to do that business in all branches, public as well as private, would increase 25 per cent.
Could the minister give the committee a statement concerning the results which have been effected by the establishment of the rural mail service?

The rural mail service brings the post office, -as it were, to the door of each inhabitant of the rural districts. The demands that we have for the establishment of rural mail delivery routes throughout Canada are evidence that the people are satisfied with the system. During this year we 'have not extended the system, and if we do not do so for some time to come it is simply on account of the stringency of the times.
Can the minister give figures showing the financial result of the service year by year from its inception?

I cannot do that now. We promised to get that information for the hon. member for Pictou, but it was impossible to get the figures 'between the time when the committee rose at six o'clock and now. I believe, however, that we can get the figures to-morrow.
I understand that the institution of this service means the general closing of post offices?
Yes.
Who is the judge of that matter, the inspector, or the department?

The matter is gone into very carefully by the superintendent of the Rural Mail Service, and upon the report made by him the department decides whether or not the rural mail route should be established and whether or not the post office should he closed.

In my constituency the first rural mail service was introduced at New Richmond.. The route started at New Richmond railway station, and included New Richmond proper, an office opened about five years ago, while New Richmond West, an office which had existed for over 60 years, was closed. The result is that the people are worse off than they were before,

and they have 'been asking the department to allow the old office to remain open. The people want to know upon what process of reasoning the department decided to close an office which had been in existence for sixty years, and to allow an office opened only three or four years ago to remain open.

Prom what the hon. member said this afternoon and this evening, it appears to me that he gives two reasons why this post office should be kept open: first, that it was established sixty years ago, and, secondly, that there is a model school near the post office, the children from which distributed the letters to the inhabitants. In the face of the report which I got, I do not think that those reasons would be sufficient for me to keep this post office open and at the same time to maintain this rural mail route. However, we are sending a special man down there to see whether or not it is expedient in the public interest that this office be closed. I know that my hon. friend would not make such an effort to have this office kept open unless there was some good reason why it should be kept open.

I do not like the explanation of the minister with regard to those people who do not ask for this rural mail service. In the case where only 50 per cent of the people say they want the service, the other 50 per cent are deprived of the post office and must necessarily take up the rural service or have no service at all.

That depends upon the circumstances. - There are some cases in which particular circumstances arise which lead us to believe that the closing of the post office would be a hardship, and not in the public interest. In these cases the post offices are not closed. A great deal of care is exercised in this matter; the interests oi everybody are gone into as far as possible before a post office is closed. Only the public interest moves us to close a post office, under the circumstances which I have mentioned. However, the practice to which my hon. friend refers has been the rule since the inauguration of the rural mail service; it is borrowed from the United States. It has worked very well; very few complaints against the rule in question have come to the department.
The fact that 50 per cent of those on rural routes have decided to ask for the rural delivery, with the experience we have had since the inauguration of the system, is
evidence to me that the rule is a good one, and that we should adhere to it.
Would the minister state the deficit in the department due to the operation of the rural delivery service?

I could not do * that
to-night.
Would the minister let us have that information to-morrow?

I will do the best I
can, but it will take a considerable amount of work because the accounts are not kept separately in the department.

It is easy to understand
that if a rural route traverses a well settled locality there is no necessity to continue the rural post office; but in the condition that prevails generally in the Prairie Provinces, where the population is established on the checker board system, the route can cover only a small proportion of those who were served by the rural post office. Special consideration should be given to these cases.

The principle laid
down by the hon. member is generally followed by the department. We have a general rule, of course, that when a rural mail route is established the rural post office is closed; but, as my hon. friend says, there are circumstances under which we cannot close the post office. Every case is examined very closely by the officers of the department, and generally by myself, and the decision depends on our view of what will best suit the interests of the locality.

All through eastern.
Nova Scotia there are very long rural mail services. The Intercolonial in the east passes through the centre of the province, and the distant points along the coast are served by coach. A small extra amount would probably induce the coach-driving people to adopt, at least in the summer, automobiles in place of the coaches. That would be a great improvement in the mail service. It is evident that in such places it would be impossible to establish the ordinary rural mail delivery, because it would take the driver of a coach, who who might possibly have to travel forty, fifty, or sixty miles, so long to call at every farm house that the people at the end oi the route, say at a place nice Canso, a town of 2,000 inhabitants, would have to wait altogether too long for their mail. A

motor service was employed between Anti-gonish and Sherbrooke, a forty-mile route. The contractor did this voluntarily, and it was found that whereas the coach reached Sherbrooke at 9 o'clock in the evening, the automobile reached there at 5 o'clock in the afternoon, after delivering the mails at the post offices along the route for forty miles. That is a very important accommodation to give to the people in those places, and I trust the minister will look into that question, and if it is found impossible to apply rural mail services to those districts that some improved accommodation of this kind will be given.

The hon. member for
Guysborough has suggested that the minister should adopt an automobile delivery.' I think it would be well for the Postmaster General to give us the cost of the maintenance of the automobile in the inspector's employ at Sherbrooke, Que., including repairs, gasolene, chauffeur, and so on, for the past year. These figures might convince the hon. member for Guysborough that an automobile service is not a practical way of delivering mail. At the same time the minister would be answering a question that I and I think the people would like to have answered, that is the cost of maintaining the automobile now in the service of the department at Sherbrooke.

I do not wish my hon. friend to misunderstand me. I do not propose that the minister should buy automobiles to do this service, but when he advertises for tenders for the service, I would like him to consider what additional amount of money would be required by the contractor to give the people this accommodation, especially in the summer season when the roads are good. If it was a small amount, and I believe it would be, the change might be made in many places. It might be found to be too extravagant to be adopted, but I do not think so. The minister is probably familiar with the way in which business is done in the country districts. Livery stable people are generally the contractors in the case of large contracts where long distances have to be covered, and the livery stable horses are very much in request in the summer time. Many people want horses to drive round to the sea shore, and on holidays, but in the winter time they are a drug on the market. It would perhaps pay the proprietors of these long distance coaches very well to put a car on in the summer

time, and to reserve their horses for other uses, or use them when the snow is deep to carry the mails. There are circumstances of that kind which I think the minister would find would reduce the cost very much, and I would ask him to investigate the matter.

What my hon. friend says is, I think, very reasonable. I understand him to say that there are certain parts of Nova Scotia where it would not be in the public interest, or in the interest of those who inhabit those parts, to establish rural mail delivery, but that it would be in, the public interest, and would probably cost no more, to open post offices nearer to each other, and have the service done by automobiles. Under ordinary circumstances, I think such a system would commend itself immediately to me, but in view of the fact that we are obliged to curtail expenditure at the present time, it is a matter which I would have to investigate before giving a definite answer. In reply to my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea), I may say that the automobile, to which he refers, was purchased before 1911, and it was an old automobile at that. It is a fact that the automobile is costing a large sum of money for repairs and maintenance, and the other day I took occasion of a visit from the inspector to instruct him to report how much 9 p.m. that automobile cost, why the cost was so great, and if it was necessary to maintain the automobile in the service. He represented to me-his report has not yet come to hand-that the automobile was a source of economy in the inspector's office at Sherbrooke. For instance, he said that with the car a man could make three or four inspections a day, while if he had not the car at his disposal, it would take three or four days to make one inspection. However, I am to get a full report on these questions, and then I will decide what to do.
An automobile might be a source of economy, but not a seven-passenger touring car.

My hon. friend is right, but as I have mentioned this was a secondhand car when it was purchased. If we can sell the car to any advantage and purchase a small car, I think it would be to the advantage of the department.

Will the minister be able to give us the information as to the cost of

maintenance, and the rest of it, before the session closes?

I hope so. I have
written again to the inspector instructing him to send me a report.	[DOT]

I would like the minister to give his attention to a matter which I regard as of considerable importance. But before touching on that, I would like to call the attention of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) to a fact in regard to the figures which he quoted in comparing the increase in the number of employees during 15 years, with the increase during the last four years. I asked him if he did not think it would be fairer to make the comparison between the increase during the past four years and the increase in the four years immediately preceding. If the number of letters posted in Canada is a criterion of the number of officials required to do the business of the post office, the increase in the number of letters posted in 1914 as compared with 1911 is equal to the total number of letters posted in 1900. But it was not in regard to that that I desired to speak. I want to take exception to the argument that we should have a surplus in the Post Office Department, that it is evidence of had management if the Post Office Department shows a deficit. With that statement I do not agree. If there is any department of the Government, which, in my judgment, is justified in having a deficit, it is the Post Office Department. Every cent of revenue in that department comes directly out of the pockets of the people, and no Postmaster General is doing his duty if he can point to a surplus in his department while the people are being imperfectly served. Give the people of the country a good service, and you will find them making no objection, if they find the balance a little on the wrong side of the ledger.
In regard to the rural districts, rural mail delivery has proved a boon; the people are delighted with it. In many country districts they have a right to ask the Government to spend some of its money in giving postal facilities. What else can the Government of this country give many people in the country districts, especially in the rougher and more poorly settled districts. Even if it costs more to give that service in certain districts the department is justified in giving it. Again and again I have made application to the department asking for services in the more sparsely
settled parts of my county, and invariably the first thing done is to look up the revenue from the post office in the district. I do not think it is right; I do not think that should be so. For instance, in many places in the county we have a bi-weekly service. In my judgment that is a little better than no service at all. The people should have at least a tri-weekly service, and, even if the revenue is not equal to the expenditure, the department would be justified in giving that service. I weuld ask the minister's consideration of the fact that by the establishment of the parcel post great hardship and great injustice were done to many people who were serving the country on certain routes. There is no doubt about that at all. Many of those people encountered pretty severe competition, and, as the Postmaster General knows, performed the services required for a very small sum of money indeed, hardly enough to pay for the food of their horses, and for the wear and tear of their rigs. They did obtain considerable revenue from the carrying of parcels, but now they are obliged to carry the parcels as mail, and that source of revenue is cut off. Many of those people, in my county, and I dare say other members can say the same thing, have asked that some consideration be shown to them in view of the circumstances. Now, if it is right that railways should receive extra pay for the extra amount of mail they carry-and if they carry extra mail they will very soon come with strong arguments for extra consideration-it does seem to me that these couriers on long routes, who, before parcel post was established, were getting very small remuneration for the service they performed, should receive fair play at the hands of the department in view of what has been taken directly out of their pockets by the establishment of parcel post. It was to impress my view that they should be given extra remuneration that I rose on this occasion. In fairness to the men, I think this question should receive the serious consideration of the minister.

This matter was ventilated in the House last year, and I think at that time I pointed, out that in every contract for carrying mail on these routes a provision was inserted that if the extra mail carried should entail the hiring of extra help, either in horses or men, the rate of pay would automatically increase. I have taken into consideration the fact
Commons
that there has been great hardship in many instances by reason of the establishment of parcel post. Every ease had been judged strictly on its merits, consistently with the duty I owe to the public. In many instances I have come to the conclusion that the rates paid should, be increased.

I should like to endorse everything that the hon. member for Fron-tenac has said. The condition he has described in his county is exactly the same in the constituency I represent, which is very largely served by rural mail delivery. Practically to repeat what he said, the contractors, bidding against each other, contracted to carry the mail at low prices. They had then the benefit of the revenue from the carriage of parcels. But now they have lost that revenue, and are compelled to carry parcels at the same rate they contracted to carry the ordinary mail. In addition to that, by reason of the recent construction of railroads, the burden on some mail routes has been tremendously increased. I would urge the minister to take these facts into consideration with respect to all that part of the prairie country where the service is principally by rural mail delivery. While I am on my feet, I will take advantage of the occasion to mention the case of the mail carrier from the town of Clyde, on the Edmonton-Athabaska line, carrying mail westerly. He stated his case to me, and it seemed a very hard case. I was given to understand that he had had to hire additional teams to carry the parcels, whereas formerly he had made a very substantial revenue by carrying them ait a fair rate. I should also like to ask the department to be more prompt in the future than it has been in the past, in taking advantage of the facilities furnished for the transport of mail by the construction of railroads. To mention one particular case, last summer, on the Peace River branch of the Canadian Northern, there was a train service twice a week. It was established in the fall of 1914, and has been running ever since. In the summer of 1915 the country traversed by this road was receiving its mail once a week by ordinary stage. Now, that is a very undesirable condition. I know it existed in that case for a considerable period. The people from month to month were expecting the change to be made, but up to the last accounts I had the change had not been made; probably it has been made by now. These delays are very disappointing to the people, and I

really do not think there is any very good reason for their existence.	On
the Dun vegan line of the Peace River railroad, the track is about completed to Grand Prairie city, and the company will put on a service as soon as the rails are laid; I fancy they are laid now.

Has the contractor
handed over the route to the railway company?
No.
The railway is not finished yet?

No, that is just the point I wish to make. That of course did not apply in the case of the Peace River branch, because that route was being operated by the company at the time I speak of. But a period always intervenes between the time the rails are laid, and the taking over of , the road by the operating company, and a service dis in fact given in that intervening time. Now, the ordinary citizen cannot see any reason

and as the representative of those citizens I am bound to say I do not see any reason myself-why a responsible organization such as a railroad or a construction company, which is running trains and carrying freight and passengers, should not be allowed to take the mails at the same time. The rails, I think, will be up to Grand Prairie city now, and the company will be conveying passengers and freight to Grand Prairie city on schedule from this time forward. And with all deference to precedent and everything else, I respectfully urge that it would be right and proper for the Post Office Department to make arrangements for having the mails carried twice a week, even before the railroad is taken over by the operating department of the company. The same applies to the branch to Peace River Crossing, and to the Waterways railroad, which is constructed as far as Lac la Biche. I do not know whether it is under the operating department or not, but a regular train service is being run at the present time. Inasmuch as the Waterways railway has track laid for 182 miles from Edmonton, and the balance to Fort McMurray will be laid during the coming summer, I would urge that means be taken to have the mails conveyed by that route, so that the construction parties on the road-the tracklaying and ballasting parties-will get the benefit of the mail service and the people at the further end will in all probability receive their

mail in shorter time than if it were taken over the present route, that is to say, by rail to Athabaska Landing, thence by steamer and then over the portage to Fort McMurray. I desire to bring these matters to the attention of the department.
There is another matter which I believe has been arranged, and if so I desire to compliment the department on making the arrangement, because they have stepped^ a little outside of the ordinary rule in doing so, and therefore they are entitled to every credit. I refer to the delivery of mail for the town of Grouard, which is situated about eight or ten miles from the line of the Dunvegan railway. The ordinary trail from Grouard strikes the railroad at a point about ten miles from the town, but there is no railroad siding thtere, and it is approximately eight or ten miles from where the trail actually touches the railroad until it reaches the railroad siding. For a considerable time the department insisted on the Grouard mail being delivered by the railroad at the High Prairie siding, and it was then taken by .stage ten miles back to where the trail crossed the road, and then ten miles further to Grouard. The people asked that the train be stopped at the crossing of the trail, and that the delivery and receipt of mail for Grouard be made at that crossing. I understand that that has been done. If it has not been done I want to say that it ought to be done.
It has been done.

If it has been done the department 'has stepped aside from its ordinary rule in order to do it. By doing so it has given a great accommodation to an important settlement, and that is what, if I may say so, I understand the department is for. I desire to give the department credit for having taken that action, and, as it was able to step aside from the ordinary rule,in that case, so it may step aside from the ordinary rule in those much more important cases of the delivery of mail at Spirit river, at Grand Prairie city over the Dunvegan line, at Lac la Biehe over the Waterways railroad and later to Fort McMurray.

Early in the session I called the minister's attention to a question in regard to the planning of rural mail route Alma No. 1 in my county, running through the districts of Sylvester and Lochbroom. As a result of that route altogether seven people living on a cross road in the district affected were deprived of any mail accommodation on account of the closing of the post office at Sylvester. I brought the, matter up some time ago and moved for the papers but they have not yet been brought down. The minister will remember that I communicated with him in regard to the matter, and I understood from him that the post office would be opened so that those people would have some place, particularly in the winter time, to get their mail I understand, however, that no action has been taken. 1 mention this as an instance of the imprudent planning out of mail routes in my county. I understand there was some reason why the assurance of the department was not carried out and I would like to know what it is.

I remember that instructions were given with reference to this matter, but I will again look into it. I am surprised if those papers have not been brought down, .because, so far as I am aware, all the papers moved for so fax have been brought down this session.

I would like to call the minister's attention to another case. I have said that a great many of the rural mail routes in my county have been laid out very imprudently; and for political considerations as the correspondence will show. I have a return brought down by the minister in regard to the establishment of a rural mail route from Eureka to Sunnybrae and return, a matter to which I referred in the House when speaking on the Budget. The minister answered a question put by an hon. member who sits behind him in regard to this route.
I have herg a letter of complaint which illustrates the way in which the rural mail routes have been laid out in my county. The route is Route No. 2, Seotsburn. It begins at Seotsburn, travels through Rogers Hill and Elmfield, and returns back a mile and a half to the road known as the Campbell road. This road, if a road at all, has from six to seven gates on it; it is not much used by the people, and it is not kept open in the winter at all. The mail carrier has to travel in front of his horse in order to make a track through the snow in the winter time. There are along the route nine families, four of whom do not want the service at all. They were perfectly satisfied with the office and with the service that was rendered before. Acting on the

advice of the people in my constituency who advise my hon. friend, the department closed up this easily accessible post office, and undertook to lay out a mail route to come by that particular road which was not used by the general public at 'all. It is all very well to talk about the glories of the rural mail service, but when rural routes are laid out under such conditions as those which I have mentioned, and post offices closed and mail routes disarranged, my hon. friend should revise very carefully the reports made to him by those who have charge of the rural mail routes in the province of Nova Scotia, and the recommendations of his political advisers in my county.
In regard to the rural mail route from Eureka to Sunnybrae, my hon. friend answered certain questions put by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) on March 9. The questions were as follows:
1.	What is the difference in cost between the railway mail service and the rural mail service actually in existence at or near the place called Sunnybrae, N.S., mentioned by the member for Pictou, pages 1304 and 1305 of unrevised Hansard ?
2.	What, if any, advantages have accrued by reason of the establishment of the rural mail service in question?
The minister made the following answers:
1. Present cost by rural mail delivery, $901; former cost by railway, $895 ; increased cost, $5.10.
Then my hon. friend went on to say that under the old system mails went up one side of the river and down the other, and that the people did not receive their mail at a satisfactory time. He also said:
In addition, these mails are delivered not at post offices some distance from the houses of the farmers, but at their doors, along the whole route, and the best proof of the usefulness of the service is that rural field officer McLeod reports through the inspector that, upon making inquiries amongst the box holde'rs, they all expressed themselves as well pleased with the rural mail delivery, and under no conditions would they wish to return to the former service.
My hon. friend the other day, in response to a motion, brought down a return which tells a story in regard to this service, and which shows that a number of people in the village of Eureka, who were anxious for a mail contract, got some of the people in that vicinity and along the riverside to sign a petition asking to have a rural mail service laid out. The circumstances previously had been, that a branch line of the Intercolonial railway ran from the station of the road in my county to a place called Sunnybrae, and on that line there were two trains

a day furnishing the people who live along the riverside with their mail service. In the villages on both sides' of the river are stores where there was post office accommodation. There was no suggestion from the people interested that there should be a change. The correspondence shows that the request for a change came from friends of the Postmaster General who *ere anxious for the job.
I am afraid I have more friends than I know of.

I hope the hon. gentleman will not be disappointed when he finds that he has fewer. I have here a return on this subject, and it shows the ridiculousness of the answers to questions given by my hon. friend. Here is the petition of residents of Sunnybrae. asking that the old system should be re-established.
We, the undersigned residents of Bridgeville. Springville and Sunnybrae, in the county of Pictou, province of Nova Scotia, respectively beg leave to present this petition :
1.	We all reside along the lines of the Sunnybrae branch of the Intercolonial railway.
2.	Up to January 1st, 1915, we received our mail daily both from East and West.
3.	On January 1st, 1915 Rural Mail Delivery came into force from Eureka to Sunnybrae. This, instead of being a benefit, has proved an injury to us, delaying our eastern mail from 24 to 36 horn's.
4.	A petition was sent to the department in favour of rural mail delivery. This was signed mostly by persons living between the places above mentioned. A counter petition was afterwards sent in signed to a large extent by the same persons who have signed this present petition, there having been no acknowledgement of the last petition sent in. Rural mail delivery is a benefit to persons residing between points above mentioned but a distinct injury and inconvenience to persons residing at any of the three villages above mentioned.
5.	The mail service formerly in force in the three villages above mentioned was . entirely satisfactory up to January 1st, 1915. We respectfully petition the department that the service be changed as soon as possible and placed upon the same or as good a basis as it was before the said 1st of January, 1915, and your petitioners will ever pray.
Dated at New Glasgow this 6th day of January, 1915.
That is signed by eighty well-known residents of villages in the nine miles between Eureka and Sunnybrae. This was referred to Mr. McLeod, whose chief occupation seems to be running around my county to find rural mail routes. The results of his administration have not been altogether happy. I could take my hon. friend to qvery one of the rural mail routes laid out in my county and show that there is a trail of dissatisfaction because of arrangements

made for political purposes, among the effects of which are that a greater or smaller number of people in every case have been entirely cut off from all mail privileges. Mr. McLeod sends a report which the minister, in good faith, gives to the House. The effect of that report is a declaration by Mr. McLeod that, though these people signed this petition-and they are intelligent men ,-they did not know what they were talking about; that he had gone there and found that these people did not want the old service. These papers disclose the further interesting fact that in the administration of this rural mail delivery other interests were affected very materially. In Guys-borough county are the post offices of Caledonia, Saint Mary's River, and others which receive their mail from Sunnybrae on the Intercolonial railway. When Mr. McLeod and the local political dignitaries in my county decided to take the mails off the railway and create this new service, they arranged also to carry the mails for these points in Guysborough county by the same carriers. The result was that Mr. Rawlings, the Conservative candidate in Guysborough, wrote an indignant letter on the subject. Evidently there was more correspondence with Mr. Rawlings, for his letter would indicate that this was only one of the complaints which he made:
I may say also that this move was wholly the idea of the department. Every man from Sunnybrae to Sherbrooke was, and still is, opposed to the connecting of the mail service with the rural mail service, and prefers to have the train connection. It was not at all in the public interest that the change should be made, and, incidentally, I would suggest that all the mail for Sunnybrae and all points between Sunnybrae and Sherbrooke be sent out from Ferrona on the train as formerly, and the mail connection from Guysborough county going West being also made with the train people of Sunnybrae and Caledonia.
According to Mr. McLeod's own report the railway carried the mails for these points from Eureka to Sunnybrae for $313 a year. In paying this money to the Intercolonial, which is also a Government institution, the Postmaster General was taking money out of one pocket of the Government and putting it into the other. This train makes close connection wit,h mails from Halifax. The mails carried by train were delivered in the post offices of the several villages before one o'clock every day. But under the new arrangement, the carrier starts from Eureka at the same time as the train does, and he has to travel nine miles up one side of the river. He does not get to Sunnybrae until long after the train gets there. Then he
has to travel nine miles down the other side of the river, and the villages on that side receive their mails still later.
To show the way this thing has been received, let me deal with the tenders for the service. There were four tenders-J. W. Russell, $1,000; Andrew McKay, $1,070; D. Fraser, $1,200 and another. They were asked if they would take a lesser amount, and all declined. Evidently, Mr. McLeod came and saw Mr. Gillespie, because that gentleman says in his correspondence that matters have been " explained " to him, and he is willing to take $800. And this is what Mr. Fraser says in one of his letters:
June 16, 1914.
Dear Sir,-I received your note yesterday, the 15th, asking my reason for putting my tender so high.
My reason is that I do not want to work for nothing. I figured out what it was going to cost me, so X thought my tender about right. It is all of 30 miles. So if you do not give it to me do not give it to a Grit as I am told some of them have put in a tender.
This man wanted $1,200 and would not come down-he put in something for his work and something for his party service.
To whom is that letter addressed?

The strange thing is that it does not show to whom it is addressed. I would like to have that made clear-whether this letter was to Mr. Tanner, or to Mr. McLeod, or to the Post Office Department. Anyway, these mails were taken off the Intercolonial railway train, where the cost of the service was only $313 a year, and they were given to Mr. Gillespie. According to my hon. friend, Mr. Gillespie gets $895 for carrying these mails; according to these papers the amount of his tender was $800. A short 'time after this service had been instituted came this petition to which I have just referred. This petition was referred to Mr. Tanner.
Who is Mr. Tanner?

He is the Conservative member for my constituency in the Provincial Legislature. He was asked what he thought about it. So far as the correspondence indicates, when Mr. Tanner got this petition signed by 85 people, he rather straddled the fence. Whatever was done, if we have all the letters here, was evidently done through Mr. McLeod, his fidus Achates. There were some very indignant letters in this correspondence;
comm6ns
some people were very angry over this contract being changed. One gentleman writes to Mr. Albert Grant as follows:
I understand you have a petition to get the mail on the train again. Please put my name to it; it is only a rat the way it is.
I do not know what he means, but he evidently uses the most emphatic word to express his objection against taking the mail service from the railway. My hon. friend paid the Intercolonial $313. The total cost of the service before was $895.84, the estimated cost of the proposed service was $800, but, according to the statement made in answer to the hon. member for Souris, the present cost of the service is $895. My hon. friend is giving a poorer service to the people along the road, and he has taken the $313 which went to the Intercolonial railway and has given it to this political contractor in Eureka. What is the good of my hon. friend talking of economizing in his department if he does things like that? I have given him three examples of absurd rural mail services in my county; I can give him many other examples of a like nature. There is no use in his talking about economizing if he is going to let Mr. McLeod run loose in Nova Scotia and accept his recommendations with regard to every suggested rural mail route. There is no sense in that kind of business. It does my hon. friend no good; it serves only to disarrange business conditions and create annoyance. It means that here and there half a dozen people are deprived of mail service altogether. I ask the minister in all seriousness to look into these matters and remedy them.

The service that has been referred to by the hon. member for Pictou is of special interest in my constituency, because it ends at Sherbrooke, in Guysborough county. I am glad that he has laid, the facts before the minister, and I trust that the road is now clear for some improvement. I was under the impression that the service in Pictou county had been improved by the establishment of a rural mail route and that that would account for the delay in connection- with the through service to my constituency, which is in charge of the same courier. But since the rural mail service in Pictou county has not improved matters, I think it ought to be abandoned, because it has injured the service very much in Guysborough county. From Sunnybrae to the town of Sherbrooke

the route is very long, and delay of one day is incurred in waiting for the man who delivers the rural mail along the East river of Pictou to get to Sunnybrae. If it is necessary to have a rural mail delivery service on the East river of Pictou that is another matter. The point is that the through mail which -runs to Sherbrooke down through the district of Caledonia should go to Sunnybrae by rail, because that is the only way in which it can get fair despatch from Sunnybrae to Sherbrooke. If the courier has to wait in Sunnybrae half a day in order to get his mail bag to go on to the route to Sherbrooke, it makes the service very slow indeed. I have received a good many letters in this matter; no person along the route from Sunnybrae to SheTbrooke seems to be satisfied with the present arrangement. They say that it is the worst service they have ever had on that route. The contractor also is complaining; he says that he has to do the whole service at night, that his passengers have deserted him, and that he is running the contract at a loss by reason of the change that has been made in the county of Pictou. A merchant doing business at Caledonia addressed the following letter to Mr. J. S. Cameron, the present contractor:
Are we going to have our mail continue and connect with that rural delivery business at Sunnybrae? What we should have is our mails connect with the train at Sunnybrae, morning and evening, as it used to. If the department wants to give the people on East River a rural delivery, let them do so. When they would not favour us with a daily they should at least give us a tri-weekly that would give us a better service than we get from present arrangements. For instance, a letter mailed in New Glasgow to-day would get to Eureka to-night, to-morrow would land at iSunybrae, and Thursday would get here, and a reply could not be sent until Saturday, which would not reach New Glasgow until Monday noon-just a week, all but one day, in transit.
The distance between New Glasgow and Caledonia is only 28 miles, of which 18 miles are covered by a railroad having a daily service. But under the present system it takes a week to send a letter from New Glasgow, which is the principal town with which these people do business, to Caledonia, and get a reply. If the minister will look into that service, he will see that it is the worst that he can find anywhere., I hope he will be -able to do something to rectify it. It has been drawn to the minister's attention that the service is costing the country more than it cost previously. $895 is being paid to the man

who carries the rural mail up and down the East river. $895.84 was the total cost of the old service, including $313 that was paid to the Intercolonial railway. The Government loses the $313 they earned by carrying this mail up and down the East river, and they are spending the whole of the amount that they spent before, save the small sum of 84 cents. No person in Pictou county is satisfied with it, and the service has been very much worse in the county of Guysborough. I think it is a case for the attention of the department.

I am a little surprised at the remarks of my hon. friend for, as far as I know, Mr. Macleod is an old and trusted employee of the department. He makes a report that three-fourths of the people along this route are satisfied. Then my hon. friends come here this evening with complaints that seem to be serious.
I took them all from the return.
All I can do is to send somebody to the locality who will make a correct and accurate report upon the situation, and if I find that the present system is not satisfactory I will change it.

Should not the officer
have thought of the inconvenience to the other end of the route when he. established it?
Mr. 'CASGRAIN: Certainly.
There must be some defect in the system if the officer does not report the whole situation to the department.
Is the minister in a position to say what revenue has been received from the war tax stamp?

It is impossible, be-,
cause we cannot make a distinction between the revenue received from war tax stamps and that from ordinary stamps.

When the tax was introduced the Minister of Finance made a strong point of the fact that the postage was not being increased, but that the two cents postage was to remain in effect. The object of the separate stamp was to have the people recognize that at was a contribution for war purposes. The separate stamp was ridiculous and it was changed; but I think the public should know exactly what they are paying for the service of the department, and what they are paying for war purposes.

The only figures I
could give are the net returns. My hon. fi'iend knows why the system of using a two-cent stamp and a one-cent stamp was changed. The change was made in response to a very general demand from the public, simply for convenience. For a long while I resisted, because I was of the opinion that, as time went on, if we were ever in a position to repeal the special tax on letters, it would be very hard to convince the Minister of Finance that we should return to the two-cent rate when we had a three-eent stamp. But after considering the matter we came to the conclusion that the best thing to do was to adopt the present two-cent stamp with the one-cent surtax on it.

On the day that the Min-itser of Finance introduced the proposal of a war stamp, the right hon. leader of the Opposition suggested that it was ridiculous to have two stamps on a letter. It took the minister and the Government a year to admit the validity of the argument of the right.hon. leader of the Opposition.
Is there no way in which the minister can tell the House how much has been collected from the sale of the war tax stamps?
My officers tell me it is impossible.
That revenue is not ear-marked or kept separate as war tax?
No.

Will the minister look into the circumstance connected with the Scotsburn rural route number -two, because I have received a lot of correspondence with regard to this route, which is situated partly in Guysborough. On one portion of the route there are three well known farmers who do quite a stock business, and who are cut off from mail accommodation altogether. The minister will see the lack of wisdqm of establishing rural routes, if people who do business are thus deprived altogether of postal service. It is all very well to say that a dozen people will get mail at their front doors, and that the majority should rule; but that is no justification for taking away from people privileges and advantages which they now enjoy.

What mail facilities are
given on the Canadian Northern Railway between Edmonton and Vancouver?
The information I have is that no facilities are now provided between those two points.

I would suggest the advisability of making provision for such accommodation without delay. The Canadian Northern railway have been operating three trains a week each way between Edmonton and Vancouver since some time in November. They give a thoroughly first-class passenger service. The time 'by that route is considerably shorter than by the other route, and of course there are points along the route that should be served. In further reference to the Dunvegan Railway Peace River service, it is the expectation that the present service of two trains a week will he changed to three trains a week at the opening of spring. I would urge the Government to take advantage of this train service to have at least as many mails as the company operates passenger and express trains. On the Waterways road to (Lac la Biche there is now a train service three times a week. There should be a corresponding mail service. The mail service beyond Lac la Biche should be established as coiistruction progresses. In regard to the service over the Canadian Northern railway, Peace river branch, I would urge very strongly that if the railroad is giving a service twice a week to San Gudo and the department is taking advantage of that service to carry the mail, the department should give a corresponding twice-a-weelt service for the balance of the route to Whitecourt. That will be the terminus of the line to which a weekly .service now goes, hut with the increase in the train service, I think there might very well be an increase in the mail service.
What portion of the money derived as revenue from the war stamps goes into the war fund?
My hon. friend knows that all the moneys collected from the sale of stamps, whether ordinary stamps or war stamps, go into the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Where do the expenditures come from?
From the same fund.

If there is a deficit in the Post Office Department, what does the war fund get out of the revenue from the sale of war stamps? Is it not the case that, but for the war stamps, the deficit would have been much greater? Do the war stamps 
not merely serve to bolster up the deficit in the Post Office Department?
No.

By taking one-third of the revenue from the sale of postage stamps at outside points, and one-half of the revenue from the sale of postage stamps in the cities, could the minister not arrive at an approximate estimate of how much is due to the war fund from the sale of stamps? If he can make such an estimate, is it not right that the money should go to the purpose for which it was intended?

While the suggestion of my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Pardee) may seem to be a means by which we could arrive at an estimate of the war stamp revenue, he must take into consideration that a great many postage stamps are sold, not only attaching to letters,
10 p.m. but as stamps for drugs, cheques, and other things subject to the war tax. We might say that 33 1-3 per cent of the revenue is derived from the war tax, but that would only be from stamps afiixed to letters and postcards.
It would be 50 per cent on post cards.

That is right, but it must be borne in mind that there is a considerable amount of mail matter to which no war stamps are affixed. It is therefore a very difficult question. It has occupied the attention of the department, but we have not been also to solve it yet.

Mr. Chairman, in the month of November, 1915, the Postmaster General introduced a postal service on the Transcontinental between Chaudiere and Monk Station. This is a section in the parish of Sainte-Perpetue, in my constituency. The innovation was gladly greeted by all the people of that country. Now, I would ask, and I think I have in that the support of my colleagues from Levis, Dorchester, Bellechasse, and Montmagny, that the service be improved. As conducted to-day, the service is satisfactory to us, but I know that many have asked and demand important improvements. We would like to have' on the mail car of the Transcontinental a clerk who would sort the mails immediately, so as to permit of a quicker distribution.
I think the Postmaster General could comply with my request, because the people of my county deserve that.

The Transcontinental has cost the country close on to 200 millions of dollars, and I think that the ratepayers have a right to get the reforms I am advocating.
Mr. CASGRAIN (Translation). I must state, for the benefit of my friend from 1'Islet (Mr. Paquet) that, as he is aware, the question of the postal service on the Transcontinental is one that has been under consideration in my department for a long time. As soon as the trains began to move on the Transcontinental we came to an understanding with the members from constituencies along the line, to give them a mail service, which is not at present as satisfactory as we should like, because the mail is carried in a baggage car. We intended to establish a postal service in connection with that line an,d carry the mail in mail cars, but, unfortunately, the railway has not sufficient material yet to allow of our putting mail cars on that section of the line.
I believe that my hon. colleague, the Minister of Railways, is negotiating to purchase the necessary material, and as soon as we get it we shall comply with the very legitimate request of my hon. friend from Tlslet, and of members from other counties along the line.

Where there is a deficit, as we have in the present report of the Post Office Department, does the revenue from the war stamps sold for letters, patent medicines, cheques, and financial transactions subject to the tax, go into the Post Office Department to help make up the deficit; or had it not gone into the Post Office Department would there not have been a greater deficit?
I repeat that there is no separate fund in the Post Office Department for the reception of the moneys collected on war stamps.
Does the Post Office Department not get credit for the revenue from those stamps?

Yes, but all the moneys collected from the sale of those stamps goes into the Consolidated Fund. It is clear that if the war stamp did not exist, there would not be so much money in the Post Office Department to meet the expenditure.
So the deficit would be much greater.

I do not say it would be.
129i

This is about the situation, is it not? Unlees the Post Office Department has a surplus equal to the amount of the war .stamps sold, the war fund gets nothing from the sale of those stamps. If the Post Office Department comes out even, independent of the sale of war stamps, the proceeds from the sale of the war stamps stand to its credit, or can be applied to war purposes. Of course, all the revenue from the Post Office Department goes into consolidated revenue, and all its expenses are paid out of consolidated revenue. If the Post Office Department, after selling the war stamps and getting the cash therefor, does not find itself in a condition to hand over its excess, it is clear that not one farthing from the sale of the stamps goes to war purposes, or any other purpose than that of the Post Office Department.

When this tax was first introduced I suggested that letters to Canadian soldiers at the front should go free of Canadian postage. I made the suggestion two or three times, and the hon. member for Rouville also intended to urge this on the Government. In his absence, through illness, I brought the matter up, but the request was turned down, the Prime Minister stating that in the absence of the Postmaster General he would not discuss the matter. I should also like to ask the Postmaster General about the mess that occurred at Montreal before the Christmas holidays last year; it would probably be in November. The people had been told that the parcels intended for the front would require certain postage, and they accordingly put the 3tamps on. A week or two afterwards, to their dismay, it was announced that all these parcels were stranded in London, and that if they were to reach the front the Canadian Government would have to make good the difference in postage. Would the minister explain what really occurred, and say whether it is likely to happen again. If our suggestions had been adopted in the first instance, it would never have happened.

I think I explained last year that it was absolutely impossible for us to allow letters to be sent to soldiers at the front without prepayment of postage. In accordance with the Postal Convention, letters would not be delivered unless properly stamped; and unless the Postal Convention was superseded by another agreement, which under present circumstances

would be very difficult, it would be impossible for us just now to give the privilege which my hon. friend suggests.
Not even through the military post offices at the front?
No. Great Britain is not doing it. I do not know whether it is in the public interest that I should divulge this, but I will tell my hon. friend what we are doing.
It is an old story now.

All letters that come
here from the front are immediately stamped in the post office on their arrival, so that the addressees will not be obliged to pay the double postage.
The soldiers are not required to stamp the letters they send to Canada?

No. With regard to the parcels that were insufficiently stamped at Montreal last year, the error occurred through information given out by an employee of the post office there as to the amount of postage required. I do not know just how the mistake occurred, but as soon as it was found out, in order to avoid any delay in the parcels reaching the front, we at once wired to England to have the necessary postage put on. This was done, and so far as we know no delay occurred. I do not think a similar error will be made again. We have reduced very considerably the postage on parcels sent to the other side. A certain portion of the postage on a parcel to the front goes to Canada, a certain portion to England and the rest to France. Now, we have relinquished the portion that is due Canada, decreasing to that extent the postage on parcels for England or France.

When we are
again in supply, woulc^ the Postmaster General give us an estimate of the number of letters mailed. during the year, and the number of postal cards issued from his department, together with an estimate for the balance of the year?
I will give the information as closely as I can.

How are we going to take these items? The Public Works Department and the Railway Department take every item in detail.
[Mr. Casgrain.3
I have no objection, but it will take a very long time.
The Public Works Estimates have the most detail; such items as bridges, strengthening of bridges, and so on.
I am prepared to give the committee all the information they desire.
I am not questioning the minister's desire in that respect. I think it has been the custom in the past to go through the items separately.
No.

That has been the custom in other departments. If the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works could put their Estimates through in bulk, as the Postmaster General suggests, it would not take nearly so much time.

As I understand it, in the past there has been free and, full discussion of all the items under the Post Office Department. The Postmaster General does not intend to close his Estimates to-night, as the hon. member for Rouville wishes to speak on some of the items. Any item will be open for further discussion later on.
That is correct.
If that is so, then this $305,000 would only be a matter of cross-entry.
That is so. Of course, we have a great many of those boxes on hand, but at a certain time we were obliged to buy a large number of boxes and to disburse that money.
It is a temporary increase in the expenditure. During the year 1914 we had to disburse this money which will come back to us in later years.
Why did my hon. friend buy so many of those boxes at one time? Why did he not purchase them as required?	-
For the reason that we got them much cheaper by making the contract under which the boxes were purchased.

I am prepared to dispute this matter of book-keeping and crossentry. The minister cannot claim that any of his deficit is accounted for by this expenditure for rural mail boxes, because it simply represents a cross-entry, an expense in which he gets his money back the moment a rural mail route is established.
My hon. friend this afternoon said in regard to another' phase of the situation that' certain proposals made by the former Postmaster General should not be criticised by us; in fact, he stated that they were accepted by us because we did not say anything about them in the House. I want to remind my hon. friend that I have a distinct recollection that, during two successive years when his predecessor was Postmaster General, he did not bring his estimates down for the consideration of the House until within the last week of the session, while every one was getting ready for prorogation. I recall that, on one occasion two nights before His Excellency came to prorogue Parliament, the Postmaster General for the first time gave the House an opportunity of discussing his estimates. Consequently my hon. friend will hardly plead that we are stopped in any way by a discussion brought on under those conditions, and I am afraid he will have to find some stronger argument to justify the course his predecessor took than to say that we on this side of the House did not prolong the session for a period beyond that when it was agreed to prorogue.
I would like to ask the minister whether he could give us any data as to how many men in the service have taken positions in the army post office and have received leave of absence. I understand there is attached to the Canadian Expeditionary Force an army post office and that quite a number of men have been given leave of absence. I would also like to know if those men, who
have been given leave of absence and who are employed in the British army post office, are receiving their pay as officials of the home department while being engaged on the post office work abroad.

I think a report was brought down the other day in which that information was given. I will ascertain that, and if it was not given in the report brought down by the Secretary of State, I will give it to my hon. friend. As to the salaries, I am not in a position to say whether they get their salaries as employees of the Post Office Department or their army pay.
I understand a letter from . a soldier at the front is franked there; that there is no stamp put upon it at the front, but that a Canadian stamp is put on here.
Yes.
There is no stamp put on in France or England.
No.
Is the stamp put on in Canada charged to any one?
The cost of making the stamp, not the face value of it, is charged to profit and loss.
If a letter can be sent from France to Canada without having a stamp on it, why is it that a letter cannot be sent from here to France undeT the same arrangement?
By virtue of the Postal Convention.
In ord,er to send a letter to the front, you must stamp it here.
Yes.

A letter leaves the front with no stamp on it, and when it arrives here you put on it a stamp that you say costs only the printing. Why cannot you send a letter to the front under the same arrangement?

If a letter is sent from here to the front when it reaches the front it has to be stamped just as we stamp it here, or the receiver would have to pay double postage. That is by virtue of the Postal Convention between the two countries.
But you have a military post office of your own. I heard Col. Creel-man in Montreal speaking about it.
It is under the authority of the British post office, not our post office.

What I cannot understand is this, the post office that you have at the front now is not under the ordinary rules of the Postal Convention; it is a military post office in charge of men whom you send over, because the letters that come from there are under their censorship and bear no stamp at all.
It is under the military authorities of Great Britain, but all the postal stations at the front are subject to the Postal Convention.

How is it. that Great
Britain allows a letter to come through without any stamp?
For the same reason that we would allow it to go through Canada; but when it gets to the receiving post office, if it is not stamped, double postage would have to be charged.
What do France and England get for the carrying of that letter if there is no stamp on it?
They do not get anything.

I have a little complaint to make to the minister. Happily, no harm resulted, as there was nothing of importance in the letter that was censored, but owing to the zeal of the censor's staff in Montreal I had a letter sent to me stamped "opened by censor."
It is the departmental censorship.

I think the zeal was not commendable because the letter was not from- the front; I think it was from the United States. I did not look on the matter as a question of carrying out orders, but as a matter of impertinence, because the letter might have contained business affairs which were none of the censor's business.
The following criticism has been made of some members of the Government, and I want to make it as mildly as I can. We are trying to get recruits; men are giving their,sons; some business men are allowing even chiefs of their staffs to go; yet some ministers have told us in the House that they refused to allow some of' their officers to go. I cannot see, for the life of me, why, for instance, a private secretary could not be replaced for the time being, if he insisted on going to the war. But one member

of the Government has told us that he declined to allow his private secretary to go. There are one or two other cases that I know of. A minister, the other night told us of an official of his department, a member of the militia for years, a first-class officer, who was anxious to go, but the minister told him he could not spare him. These things do not help recruiting. If the ministers cannot put up with a bit of inconvenience by allowing their officials to go, .how can they expect men who, perhaps, are not so closely in touch with the great necessity' to allow their sens to go. This criticism is made particularly in some parts of Ontario where recruiting is urged very strongly at this time.

Some time last summer I wrote to the minister with respect to the mail service along the Intercolonial in my own county. The minister promised to give consideration to the matter I referred to, but so far I do not think that anything has been done. The point to which I called attention is the desirability and possibility of a daily mail service for those places which are on a railway served by a daily train. The expense of a daily service as against a service three times a week in such cases would be merely trivial. Take, for instance, the case of a place like George's Eiver, in my county. A letter from Halifax addressed to a man in George's Eiver, may be carried right past the door of the addressee to Sydney, where it stays, perhaps, for two or three days, and 1 then finds its way back to George's Eiver. Not only in my part of the country but everywhere in Canada where there is the daily railway service, there should bg, as much as possible, a daily mail service. .Many people subscribe for a daily newspaper, but a newspaper two or three days old is not read. I renew my request to the minister, as far as my own county is concerned, and I have no doubt that other places along the Intercolonial are in the same position.
I wish to register my complaint and protest against this rural mail delivery business. Putting the case without adornment,
1 think that no Postmaster General should plunge into rural mail delivery with a deficit in his department. If any part of the country is to have the luxury of rural mail delivery, it ought to be only when there i6 plenty of money to provide that service. If any rural mail route has been established since the war began, especially since the last of March, 1915, when the

minister must have known that he had a deficit of something over $2,000,000, the establishment of that rural mail route was not made advisedly. As to my own part of the country, until we have a daily mail everywhere where such a mail can be reasonably provided, there is no justification for rural mail delivery anywhere. I come from a part of the country with fairly large towns and good communities. I have never asked for a rural mail delivery. I think that if we have a daily mail to post offices at reasonable distances of two miles or two miles and a half apart, we are reasonably well served, and we should not plunge into debt to the extent of the enormous deficit of last year and the one we are likely to have this year in order to provide the luxury of rural mail delivery. It will not strike the average countryman with satisfaction to be told that his postal rates are increased from two cents to three cents in order that some people in a part of the country he knows nothing about may have rural mail delivery. It would be harsh to say of the ministers that they have got money under false pretences, and I do not wish to say it. When they told the people that they must pay an extra cent on every letter in order to help in carrying on the war, the people were pleased to pay the money, at least they did not object to paying it, for such a purpose. But when it turns out that not half a cent of that money ever found its way, or ever will find its way, into the fund for carrying on the war, if that is not obtaining money from the people under false pretences, at least it is obtaining it from them in a way different from that which was explained to them, and different from that which they unduerstood.
I wish to bring to the attention of the minister another matter relating to the mail arrangements in my county. A change in the routes of the Intercolonial has disarranged one mail route. There \^as a daily mail route between the town of North Sydney and the Bras d'Or district. There was a change on the Intercolonial, and in stead of the mail to Big Bras d'Or, Little Bras d'Or and other points being delivered at North Sydney, it is delivered aj; Little Bras d'Or, three miles west of North Sydney, and does not go to North Sydney at all. The mail starts for northern points from Little Bras d'Or instead of from North Sydney as it used to. There is a hiatus there, a space of four miles where there is no mail route at all. A newspaper published at North Sydney, on Wednesday that used to
go to Bras d'Or the same night now does not reach Bras d'Or until Friday morning, on account of this break. What I want the minister to do, if it has not already been done, is to see that some arrangement is made by which the mail may be carried from North Sydney and Sydney to a point on the railway where it can be deliered for the northern district. The expense would be trivial, but the delay that is now incurred is causing a good deal of discontent among the people.
I cannot help adding my approval to what has been said by the hon. member for Fron-tenac about the hardship that is imposed upon the mail contractors. A good deal of that hardship is complained of in our part of the country, where contracts were given out for the carrying of the mail before the parcel post system was inaugurated. They complain that their vehicles are piled up with heavy loads, whereas before this new departure was made, the weight was but trifling. I need not tell the minister that the contract entered into by these men was that they were to carry the mails and nothing else. By reason of the additional material which they are now required to carry, the weight of their loads has been trebled. It was never in the minds of the parties at the time they made the contracts that they would have to carry that extra weight.' I do not know how the minister can figure it out, but I think something should be done to even up matters and to give these men compensation for the extra service that they are rendering to the country.

Deficits, of course, are always unfortunate, but if there is a deficit anywhere, it is a fair place tp have it in the Post Office Department. The criticism from the other side of the House today has come almost entirely from gentlemen who live in cities, and who have their mail delivered to them every day, for which service the whole country has been paying. I think it is only fair that the farmers of this country and those who live at some distance from the towns, should have their turn, and that, even if there is a deficit, the people in the cities should be willing to pay in order tlhat the people in the country may be accommodated. We hear a great deal to-day about keeping the boys and girls on the farm. That is a splendid sentiment, one that needs, perhaps, more consideration than has ever been given to it. One of the best ways to keep the boys and girls on the farm is to

give them the daily press. I think that this does not work out just the same in the country from which my hon. friend comes as it does in the western country. I have not been in Nova Scotia for a long time, but I should think that in the country from which my hon. friend comes no people are very distant from a town or a train. But in our country, where we have, as the 'hon. member for Edmonton has said, the checker-board or township system, it is not so easy for the people to get their mails. People to-day are anxious to get the daily paper; they aTe willing to drive miles to get it. My hon. friend said that unless there was plenty of money in the treasury we should not extend the rural mail delivery service. I have established some rural mail delivery routes in 'the constituency of Souris, and I can say that no other service is giving the people as much satisfaction - as the rural mail delivery. Having regard to the fact that we want to keep the boys and girls on the farm, I believe that even if we do run a little into debt, there is nothing that would satisfy the people like the rural mail delivery service.
